Deep-sea smelt Glossanodon semifasciatus exhibits life-history traits that reflect its mesopelagic environment and relatively low metabolic demands. Individuals captured during survey trawls in the Sea of Japan attain an asymptotic body length of 22.7 centimeters [Li = 22.7 centimeters] based on length-frequency analysis of older specimens. The onset of sexual maturity is marked by a shift in body size, with individuals first developing mature gonads when they reach a total length of 13 centimeters [Lp = 13 centimeters]. A length-weight relationship established for this species yields an estimated wet weight at that pubertal length of 11.8 grams [Wwp = 11.8 grams], whereas fully grown females achieve a maximum wet weight of approximately 69 grams [Wwi = approximately 69 grams] according to the same allometric equation. These values place G. semifasciatus among the smaller-bodied members of the family Argentinidae, consistent with its position as a zooplanktivore feeding primarily on copepods and krill throughout its life.

Reproductive investment in the deep-sea smelt is moderate relative to body size, in line with patterns observed in other temperate mesopelagic fishes. Under the thermal regime of its habitat, at a stable water temperature of 14.1 °C [T = 14.1 °C], the gonadosomatic index (GSI) averaged 7% [GSI = 7%] during the spawning season. This value falls within the range reported for iteroparous species that produce multiple batches of small pelagic eggs rather than a single high-investment clutch. Histological examination of preserved ovaries confirms asynchronous oocyte development, with multiple cohorts of vitellogenic oocytes present simultaneously.

Early life stages of Glossanodon semifasciatus are characterized by a small initial size and a protracted developmental period. Based on an assumed egg diameter of 800 micrometers derived from congeneric Argentina sphyraena, the estimated wet weight at birth for a newly hatched yolk-sac larva is 0.000268 grams [Wwb = 0.000268 grams], a value reflecting the modest maternal investment per offspring. This tiny alevin relies on its endogenous yolk reserves during the first days after eclosion before transitioning to exogenous feeding. The egg stage itself is brief; fertilized ova are likely pelagic and drift within the mixed layer, where temperatures remain near 14.1 °C [T = 14.1 °C] throughout the incubation period. Newly emerged larvae measure only a few millimeters and are morphologically underdeveloped, possessing unpigmented eyes and an incompletely formed mouth at the moment of chorion rupture.

Life-history theory predicts a predictable relationship between body size, maturation timing, and overall longevity in teleost fishes. For deep-sea smelt inhabiting waters at 14.1 °C [T = 14.1 °C], the time interval from birth to the attainment of sexual maturity is estimated at 730 days [tp = 730 days], a relatively prolonged juvenile phase compared to small epipelagic species. This extended maturation period likely reflects the slow growth rates imposed by the cold, food-limited environment of the mesopelagic zone. Once mature, individuals continue to grow slowly throughout adult life, accumulating body mass and length incrementally. Field recapture data and otolith-based aging studies further indicate that the maximum lifespan of wild individuals spans approximately 5,840 days (5840 days) [am = 5840 days], including the entire juvenile and adult phases under the same prevailing temperature of 14.1 °C [T = 14.1 °C].

Comparative analyses within the Argentine family help contextualize the demographic parameters of Glossanodon semifasciatus. While smaller-bodied argentines such as Argentina sphyraena have been documented to reach lifespans around 16 years [am = around 16 years] at similar environmental temperatures, the deep-sea smelt appears to exhibit a slightly faster pace of life, with a maximum longevity of roughly 16 years [am = roughly 16 years] based on age-length key at a temperature of 14.1 °C [T = 14.1 °C] at a temperature of 14.1 °C [T = 14.1 °C]s. The transition to first spawning, occurring after the individual has completed its somatic growth phase and accumulated sufficient energy reserves, synchronizes with the seasonal spring bloom in the Sea of Japan. Adults are thought to be iteroparous and capable of spawning annually for several consecutive years, given the absence of mass post-spawning mortality observed in some semelparous fishes. Continued monitoring of population age structure will clarify whether environmental variation imposes constraints on this general life-history schedule.
